p: I'm Kuzey Aydın, and I'm a Windborn: the winds talk to me, and if I ask nicely, they help.

My grandmother, Nermin, is the Keeper of an ancient secret. Seven bronze Keys hold the hearts of the seven great winds, and whoever brings them all together at the Gate of Seven Winds will control the weather of the whole world. A man named Mordecai Vane, who has a hand made of cold gray stone, kidnapped her to make me find the Keys for him.
In Istanbul, my cousin Ela, my best friend Bora and I found the first Key, the Yıldız, the North Wind. It lives inside me now.

In Greece, with Ela's dad, Uncle Tarık, we followed a clue from the Tower of the Winds to the island of Crete. Under the palace of Knossos, we made friends with a Minotaur, and Bora set a bronze giant named Talos free. We found the Lodos Key, the warm southwest wind.
And then I had to give it away. Mordecai's son, Vex, froze Uncle Tarık in a block of ice and made me choose. I chose my uncle.
So the score is one to one.

But Mordecai's daughter, Vera, keeps helping us in secret. And Bora has discovered that he can understand what animals are feeling. And on the leather map of the Seven Winds, a new star is glowing at the top of the world.
Iceland. Land of fire and ice.
**Kuzey Aydın,** 11. A Windborn. Carries the North Wind inside him. Getting better at asking nicely.
**Ela Aydın,** 12. Kuzey's cousin. Keeper of the Clue Book, which is now held together with tape.
**Bora Kaya,** 11. Kuzey's best friend. Can understand animals, sort of. Owns a very puffy orange coat.
**Uncle Tarık.** Ela's dad. Archaeologist. Now carries a very large umbrella.
**Grandma Nermin.** The Keeper. Held prisoner in a gray tower by the sea.
**Mordecai Vane.** Leader of the Ashen Circle. Holds the Lodos Key in his stone hand.
**Vex Vane,** 13. Mordecai's son. Has gray marks on his fingertips that are spreading.
**Vera Vane,** 13. Mordecai's daughter. Secretly returned the map. Nobody knows whose side she is on. Maybe not even Vera.

chapters.t: Chapter One: The Coldest Place I've Ever Been
p: I am the North Wind's favorite person, and I was still freezing.

Iceland at the end of November is dark for most of the day. When we landed at Keflavík airport at eleven in the morning, it looked like midnight. Snow blew sideways across the runway, and the wind howled so hard that the plane wobbled like a jelly on a plate. Three people screamed. Bora said a prayer. I said "please, please, please" to the wind under my breath, and it said *oh, all right,* and the plane landed with a bump.

The Icelandic wind was nothing like the chatty old men of Athens or the lazy cat-wind of Crete. It was huge and slow and wild, and it spoke in deep, rumbling words, very far apart, like a giant talking in its sleep.
*Windborn,* it rumbled. *Long. Have you. Been coming.*
"Hello," I said politely, through the window of the plane.
*The Black Wind,* it rumbled. *Waits. In the ice.*
And then it said nothing else at all for an hour.

"The Black Wind," I told the others in the rental car, while Uncle Tarık tried to remember which side of the road to drive on. (In Iceland it's the right side, like Turkey, so I don't know why he was confused. He said it was "the general atmosphere.") "That's the Karayel. The northwest wind."

"Kara means black," said Ela, writing in the Clue Book. "In the old Turkish wind rose, the northwest wind is called the black wind because it brings dark storms. Sudden ones. The fishermen are scared of it."

Bora was wearing his huge orange coat, plus a second coat he had borrowed from Uncle Tarık underneath it, plus two hats, plus a scarf his grandmother had knitted that went around his neck five times, plus mittens shaped like bears. Only his eyes were visible, peeking out between the scarf and the hats.
"I can't feel my face," he said. "Is my face still there?"
"Probably," said Ela.
We drove out of the airport into a landscape that looked like another planet.

Black lava fields, stretching away forever, covered in green moss and snow, lumpy and strange, like a giant had spilled chocolate pudding and then it froze. Steam rising out of cracks in the ground, as if the earth was breathing. Mountains like sleeping animals, white and gray and black. No trees at all. Not one. Ela said the Vikings cut them all down a thousand years ago and they never grew back.

And in the dark sky, when the clouds tore open for a moment, there was green light. Swirling like ribbons. Ripples of green and purple, moving slowly across the stars, like curtains blowing in a window.
"The northern lights," whispered Uncle Tarık, and nearly drove into a sheep.
The sheep looked at us with great contempt and walked slowly across the road.
I stared up at the lights. They were the most beautiful thing I had ever seen. They moved like they were alive. Like they were dancing to music I couldn't hear.
And for a second, I could have sworn the lights moved into the shape of a face.
A thin face. With too many teeth.
Then the clouds closed, and it was gone.
I didn't say anything. But I pulled Grandma's scarf up over my nose, and I didn't look at the sky again for the rest of the drive.
We stayed that first night in Reykjavík, the capital of Iceland, in a guesthouse run by an old Icelandic woman called Guðrún.

Reykjavík is the smallest capital city I have ever seen. It's more like a big village by the sea, with houses painted red and yellow and blue and green, with tin roofs, and a giant white church on a hill that looks like a rocket ship made of organ pipes. In the dark, with the snow falling and all the windows glowing yellow, it looked like a Christmas card.

Guðrún's guesthouse was a little red house with a tin roof, full of knitted blankets and wooden furniture and photographs of very serious Icelandic people with very big beards. Guðrún herself was about eighty years old, tiny, with white hair in two long braids just like Ela's, bright blue eyes, and a sweater with a pattern of reindeer.
She took one look at us, shivering in her doorway, and said, "Soup. Now."
It was lamb soup with potatoes and carrots, and it was the best soup in the history of the universe. Bora ate four bowls. Guðrún watched him with great approval.
"A good boy," she said. "Eats properly. Not like the tourists. The tourists eat salad." She said the word *salad* the way other people say the word *spider.*
Then she brought out dessert. It was a bowl of something white and creamy, like thick yogurt, called skyr, with blueberries on top. Bora said it was like Cretan yogurt "but braver."
And then she brought out something else.
It was a little plate with small cubes of something grayish-white on it, with toothpicks stuck in them. It smelled. It smelled *terrible.* Like a toilet that a fish had died in.

"Hákarl," said Guðrún proudly. "Fermented shark. A traditional Icelandic food. The Vikings ate it. You bury the shark in the ground for three months, then hang it up to dry for five months. Very healthy. Try."
We all looked at the plate.
Nobody moved.
Then Bora, who has never in his life said no to food, slowly reached out and picked up a cube.
"Bora," said Ela. "You don't have to."
"I do," said Bora solemnly. "It's for my country. For Turkey. For the honor of Turkish eaters everywhere."
He put the cube in his mouth.
He chewed.
His face went through several colors. White. Pink. Green. A sort of purple. His eyes watered. His nose ran. He made a sound like a cat that has swallowed a bee.
Then he swallowed.
There was a long silence.
"Well?" said Guðrún.
Bora wiped his eyes. He took a deep breath. "It's," he said, his voice very high, "very... interesting."

Guðrún threw back her head and laughed so hard that her braids shook. Then she poured Bora a glass of something from a bottle in the cupboard, which turned out to be just very strong blueberry juice, and slapped him on the back.
"A true Viking," she said. "I like this one. The tourists spit it out."
Bora looked very proud and very sick at the same time.
After dinner, we sat by Guðrún's fire, wrapped in knitted blankets, drinking hot chocolate. Outside, the wind howled and the snow hissed against the windows. And Guðrún told us stories.
"You are going to the countryside, yes?" she said. "Then you must know about the hidden folk."
"The hidden folk?" asked Ela, getting out the Clue Book.

"The elves," said Guðrún, completely seriously. "They live in the rocks. Big rocks, in the lava fields. You must never throw stones at those rocks, or build a road through them, or they will be angry. Here in Iceland, when we build a new road, we sometimes ask the elves first. Really. Sometimes the road goes around."
"Do you believe in elves?" asked Bora.
Guðrún looked at him with her bright blue eyes. "I don't *not* believe in them," she said. "There is a difference."

Then she told us about the Yule Lads, thirteen naughty brothers who come down from the mountains one by one in the thirteen nights before Christmas. Each one has his own bad habit. One steals sausages. One licks the spoons. One slams doors all night. One peeks through windows. One steals the candles.

"And their mother," said Guðrún, lowering her voice, "is Grýla. A giant troll woman, with hooves and a tail and a big sack. She comes down from the mountains every Christmas, looking for naughty children. To put in her sack. To put in her stew."
Bora pulled his blanket up to his nose.

"But the most important thing to know about trolls," said Guðrún, leaning forward, so the firelight lit up her face from below, "is this. They live in the dark. In caves, in the mountains, under the ice. They come out only at night. Because trolls hate the sun more than anything in the world."
"Why?" whispered Ela.

"Because if the sun touches a troll," said Guðrún, "the troll turns to stone. Forever." She pointed out of the window, into the dark. "All over Iceland, there are rocks that look like people. Like giants. Like monsters. Those were trolls, who stayed out too late, and forgot to go home before sunrise. Down by Vík, on the black beach, there are three tall rocks standing in the sea. Those were three trolls, trying to pull a ship to shore. The sun came up, and..." She clapped her hands. "Stone."
The fire crackled. The wind moaned in the chimney.
"Those are just stories," said Uncle Tarık. But he didn't sound very sure. After Talos and the Minotaur, none of us were very sure about anything anymore.
Guðrún smiled.

"Of course, professor," she said. "Just stories." She stood up and collected our cups. "But if you go into the mountains, children, make sure you are home before dark. And if you ever meet a troll..." She paused at the kitchen door. "Keep it talking until the sun comes up."
§CLUE If you ever meet a troll, keep it talking until the sun comes up. (Guðrún.)
Before we left Reykjavík, Guðrún made us go swimming.
"Everyone in Iceland goes swimming," she said. "Every day. Even in winter. *Especially* in winter. It's the law."
"Is it really?" asked Bora.
"It should be," said Guðrún, which is exactly what Uncle Tarık had said about the Parthenon. I was starting to think all grown-ups said that.

So at eight in the morning, in the pitch dark, with snow falling, we walked to the public swimming pool down the road. It was outdoors. Completely outdoors. A big blue pool, steaming in the freezing air, with lights under the water so it glowed like a jewel in the dark. Around it were smaller round pools, called hot pots, each one a different temperature: warm, hot, very hot, and one that was ice cold, for people who were completely crazy.

The water came from deep under the ground, Guðrún said. Heated by volcanoes. All of Reykjavík was heated by volcanoes. Even the pavements, in some streets, had hot water pipes underneath, so the snow melted.
The hard part was getting from the changing room to the pool. You had to walk across about ten meters of freezing concrete, in your swimming costume, with snow falling on you.
Bora went first. He ran screaming the whole way and jumped into the nearest hot pot with a splash that emptied half of it.

I went second. I didn't scream. The North Wind inside me thought the cold was lovely. The snow landed on my shoulders and didn't even melt. I walked slowly across the concrete, and an old man in the hot pot watched me with his eyebrows raised very high.
Then I got into the hot pot. And it was wonderful.

Hot water up to my chin. Snow falling on my face. Steam rising all around, glowing in the lights. The sky above dark and full of snowflakes, spinning down out of nowhere. It was like being in a warm bath on the moon.

The hot pot was full of Icelandic people. Old men talking about politics. Mothers with babies. A group of kids about our age, laughing and splashing. And they all talked to each other. That's what the hot pots are for, Guðrún told us later. Talking. Everyone sits in the hot water and talks. About the weather, about the news, about their neighbors. It's like a café, but wetter.
One of the kids, a boy with white-blond hair and a lot of freckles, swam over to me. He was about my age.
"You're not from here," he said, in perfect English.
"Turkey," I said.
"Cool," he said. He looked at me for a while. Then he said, "Your breath is weird."
I looked down. I had been breathing out, without thinking about it, and my breath was coming out as little white clouds. That was normal, in the cold. Everyone's breath was white.
But mine was sparkling. Tiny ice crystals, glittering in the light, falling into the water and floating there like glitter.
"Um," I said. "It's... a Turkish thing."
The boy thought about this. Then he nodded seriously, as if this made perfect sense.
"Cool," he said again. "Do you know about the trolls?"
"A bit," I said.
"My grandfather saw one," said the boy. "When he was young. Up in the mountains. He says it asked him the time." He shrugged. "Nobody believes him."
"I do," I said.
The boy looked at me with surprise. Then he grinned. He had a gap in his front teeth.

"My name's Siggi," he said. "If you meet a troll, don't tell it the time. My grandfather did, and it said, 'Oh no, almost sunrise!' and ran away so fast it knocked down a wall. He says if he'd kept it talking for five more minutes, he'd have a troll statue in his garden."
He swam away to his friends.
I sat in the hot water with the snow falling on my face, and thought about that for a long time.
*Keep it talking until the sun comes up.*
The first clue was on the leather map.

When we unrolled it on Guðrún's kitchen table the next morning, we saw that next to the glowing star over Iceland, there was a tiny drawing. So small that we had never noticed it before. A rock, split in two down the middle, with a line between the halves.

"Þingvellir," said Uncle Tarık, which is pronounced something like *THING-vet-leer.* "It has to be. The Rift Valley. It's where two continents are pulling apart. North America on one side, Europe on the other. They move away from each other two centimeters every year. There's a huge crack in the earth, kilometers long, and the Vikings held their parliament there, the Althing, more than a thousand years ago. The oldest parliament in the world."
§CLUE A tiny drawing on the leather map, next to Iceland's star: a rock split in two.
"Parliament?" said Bora. "Vikings had a parliament? I thought they just hit each other with axes."
"They did both," said Uncle Tarık. "Sometimes on the same day."

Guðrún packed us a huge bag of sandwiches, a thermos of hot chocolate, a thermos of soup, a bag of dried fish and four extra pairs of woolen socks. She hugged each of us at the door. When she hugged me, she whispered something in my ear.

"Your grandmother stayed in this house," she said. "Forty-five years ago. She sat in the same chair you sat in. She told me you would come." She stepped back and looked at me with her bright blue eyes. "She told me, 'He will hear the wind, Guðrún. Feed him well.'"
I stared at her. "You *knew* her?"
"I know many things," said Guðrún, and winked, and closed the door.

We drove out of Reykjavík in the blue half-light of the late morning. At this time of year, in Iceland, the sun doesn't really rise. It just sort of peeks over the edge of the world for a few hours, low and pale, and turns the sky pink and blue and gold, like a sunrise that goes on all day without ever finishing.
Þingvellir was an hour's drive away. When we got there, we parked by an empty visitor center and walked down a path into the rift.
It was like walking into a giant crack in the world.

Walls of black rock rose on both sides of us, tall and jagged, like the earth had been ripped open by giant hands. The path ran between them, down the middle of the crack, deep and narrow. Snow lay on every ledge. Icicles as long as my arm hung from the rocks. Our footsteps squeaked on the snow.
And everything was silent. Completely silent. No birds. No cars. No wind, even. Just our breathing, and the squeak of our boots.
"On that side," said Uncle Tarık, in a whisper, pointing at the wall on our left, "is North America. And on that side," pointing right, "is Europe. We are standing between two continents."
"Which continent are we on?" asked Bora.
"Neither," said Ela. "We're in the gap."
Then something said, "KRAA! Strangers! Strangers in the rift!"
A raven sat on a rock above us.

A huge one. Bigger than any bird I'd ever seen, except maybe the eagles in the zoo. Black as ink from the top of its head to the tips of its claws, with feathers that shone purple and blue in the pale light. It had clever, shiny black eyes, a thick beard of feathers under its chin, and a beak like a knife.
It was looking straight at us.
"Did that bird," said Bora slowly, "just say *strangers?*"
"It said *kraa,*" said Ela. "Ravens say kraa. It's a normal raven noise."

"No," said Bora. His eyes, between his hats and his scarf, had gone very wide. "No, it said 'Strangers in the rift.' I heard it. And now it's saying..." He listened. His eyes went even wider. "It's saying, 'The fat one has food in his pocket.'"
There was a pause.
Then Bora looked deeply offended. "Hey!" he shouted up at the raven. "I'm not fat! I'm wearing *three coats!*"
The raven tilted its head to one side. It hopped along the rock, closer, and peered down at Bora with one shiny eye, then the other.
"KRAA," it said. And this time, I almost heard the words too. Almost. Like a radio not quite tuned in. "The fat one understands. The fat one understands Krummi!"
We all stared at Bora.
Bora stared at the raven.
"Bora," said Ela, very carefully, the way you'd talk to someone holding a bomb. "Can you understand what that bird is *saying?* Not feeling. Saying. Actual words."

"I..." Bora pulled down his scarf. His face was pale. "I don't know? Yes? It's not like the Minotaur. With Asterion, it was feelings. Like a color in my head. This is... this is *words.* Real words. In Turkish. Sort of. Like when you watch a film with the subtitles on." He looked at the raven. "Is that weird? That's weird."
"KRAA," said the raven, sounding pleased. "Very weird. Krummi likes weird."
"It says it likes weird," Bora translated faintly.
The raven spread its huge wings and dropped down off the rock. It landed on the snow right in front of Bora with a soft thump, folded its wings, and looked up at him, its head on one side.
"Krummi," said Bora. "Is that your name?"
"Krummi is Krummi," said the raven. Or, Bora said it said. "All the ravens in Iceland are called Krummi by the humans. Very lazy. But Krummi is the *real* Krummi. The best Krummi. The cleverest."
"It says it's the cleverest raven in Iceland," Bora said.
"Of course it does," muttered Ela.
Bora sat down on a rock. His legs didn't seem to be working properly.

"I always liked animals," he said. "Always. Dogs come up to me in the street. Cats sit on me. At the zoo, when I was six, a goat ate my whole lunch and then followed me around for an hour. My mom says I have animal magnets." He looked down at the raven, who was examining his boots. "But I never heard them before. Never. Not until the Minotaur. And now this."
"Your great-grandmother," said Uncle Tarık suddenly.
We all turned to look at him. He was frowning, staring at the black rock walls, the way he does when he's trying to remember something from a very old book.
"Bora, wasn't your great-grandmother from Kars? In the far east of Turkey?"
"Yes," said Bora. "My mom's grandmother. Büyük Nene. She died before I was born. Why?"

"I remember Mum talking about her," said Uncle Tarık slowly. "Years ago. When I was a boy. Mum used to tell stories about the people in the Order, and I thought they were just fairy tales. And there was one about a woman from Kars. A shepherd's daughter. She could talk to wolves. They used to come down from the mountains in the winter and sit outside her door, and she would talk to them, and they would never touch her sheep." He looked at Bora. "Mum called her a Beastspeaker."
"A Beastspeaker," Ela breathed. She was writing so fast her pencil was smoking.
"I always thought it was a story," said Uncle Tarık. "But then, I thought the Minotaur was a story too."
Bora was very quiet.

"Mom has a photo of her," he said, finally. "Büyük Nene. In her living room. An old lady with a scarf, and a big smile, and a dog sitting next to her. A huge white dog. A Kangal. My mom says the dog followed her everywhere for twenty years and slept across her doorway every night." He swallowed. "I always thought it was just a nice photo of an old lady with a dog."
"Maybe it is," I said. "And maybe she was talking to it."
The raven made a soft, clicking sound in its throat.
"It says," Bora translated, "that it's very sorry about my great-grandmother. And that it would like a cheese sandwich now, please."
That made everyone laugh, and the strange tight feeling in the air went away.
The raven puffed up its feathers proudly. "Krummi knows things," it said. "Krummi knows *many* things. Krummi knows where the Black Wind's rune is hidden. Krummi will tell."
It looked meaningfully at Bora's pocket.
"For the cheese."

Bora took out the cheese sandwich that Guðrún had made. It was a beautiful sandwich, thick and soft, with butter and cheese and slices of lamb. He looked at it for a long moment. Then he gave it to Krummi. All of it.
Which, for Bora, is the greatest sacrifice possible.
Krummi ate it in three gulps. Then it hopped up onto a rock, and then onto another, along the foot of the rift wall.
"Follow!" it croaked. "The old stone with the scratches. Krummi's great-great-great-grandmother watched a strange woman hide it there. Long ago. When the strange woman was young."
My heart jumped. "What did the woman look like?"

"KRAA! Silver hair, even then. Sharp eyes. A necklace with a bronze needle." The raven sighed happily. "She gave Krummi's great-great-great-grandmother a whole sausage. A *whole* one. The ravens of Þingvellir still talk about it. A legend."
"Grandma," I whispered. "It was Grandma."
The raven led us along the rift, past a frozen waterfall that hung down the black rocks like a giant white beard, to a mossy boulder at the foot of the wall, half buried in snow.
It looked like nothing. Just a big gray rock, covered in moss and snow, like thousands of other rocks in Iceland.
"Here," said Krummi. "Krummi has led. Krummi is magnificent."

I knelt down and brushed away the snow with my mittens. Under the snow, the moss. Under the moss, the stone. And on the stone, marks. Carved lines. Straight lines and angles, like little sticks, arranged in rows.
"Runes," said Ela, kneeling next to me. "The old Viking alphabet. They didn't have curved letters. Everything was straight lines, so it was easy to carve in wood and stone."
Uncle Tarık knelt down on my other side, so excited that his glasses fogged up. He wiped them on his scarf and looked again.

"Elder Futhark runes," he said. "Very old. But mixed with something else. Look here." He pointed to a different kind of mark, a symbol like a little arrow with a hook on it. "That's not a rune. That's an Old Turkish letter. From the Orkhon inscriptions! The oldest Turkish writing in the world, from Mongolia, thirteen hundred years ago!" He looked like he might faint with happiness. "Vikings and Turks. On the same stone. Do you know what this *means?* Nobody will believe this. *Nobody.*"
"The Order of the Compass Rose was everywhere," I said. "Vikings and Turks, Greeks and Egyptians. All working together."
"For nine hundred years," said Ela softly. "To keep the winds safe."

It took Uncle Tarık and Ela an hour, a thermos of hot chocolate and most of a notebook to translate it. They sat in the snow with the Clue Book between them, arguing about every symbol. Uncle Tarık knew the runes. Ela knew how to solve puzzles. Together, they were unstoppable, although very loud.

Bora and Krummi had a long conversation about cheese in the meantime. It turns out ravens have very strong opinions about cheese. Krummi likes it "old and smelly." Bora prefers "white and salty." They agreed to disagree.
I walked a little way along the rift and talked to the wind. It was still asleep, mostly. But when I asked it about my grandmother, it stirred.
*The silver one,* it rumbled, from very far away. *She sang. To the stone. Long ago. We remember.*
"She sang?"
*To make us remember,* it said. *So that when you came, we would know you. She sang your name. Before you were born.*
I stood there in the snow between two continents, and I didn't know what to say.
"Kuzey!" Ela called. "We've got it!"
She read it out, her breath steaming in the cold air:
§CLUE Where the earth breathes boiling breath and counts to seven, wait for the white tower. When it falls, the way to the Black Wind opens under the ice that never melts.

"The earth breathes boiling breath," said Ela. "That's easy. A geyser! Iceland is full of them. Hot springs that shoot boiling water into the air. The most famous one is Strokkur. It's in a valley about an hour from here. It erupts every few minutes."
"And 'the white tower' is the water shooting up," said Uncle Tarık. "That makes sense. It looks like a white tower for a second, and then it falls."
"Counts to seven?" said Bora.
"Maybe we wait for the seventh eruption," I said. "And something happens."
"And 'the ice that never melts,'" said Ela, frowning at the page. "A glacier, maybe? Iceland has lots of glaciers. But which one?"
Krummi, who had been sitting on Bora's shoulder, suddenly flapped his wings and croaked very loudly.
"KRAA! KRAA!"
"What's he saying?" I asked.
Bora listened. His face changed.
"He says," Bora said quietly, "the gray men are coming. Three cars. Black ones. On the road above the rift. He saw them from the sky." He paused. "He says the fat one should run."
"Stop calling me fat," he added, to Krummi.
But we ran.
We ran back up the path, out of the rift, slipping and sliding on the snow. At the top, I looked back.

Three black cars were parked on the road on the far side of the valley. Gray figures were getting out. Many of them. They stood in a line on the edge of the rift, looking down. Even from so far away, I could see the frost spreading out from their feet across the snow.
We piled into our little rental car. Krummi flew in through the open door and sat on the dashboard like he owned it.
"Krummi comes too," said Bora. "He says we need him. He says we're very bad at Iceland."
"He's not wrong," said Ela.
Uncle Tarık started the engine with shaking hands. The car slid on the icy road, spun its wheels, and then shot forward. Behind us, the three black cars were starting their engines too.
"Which way to the geyser?" Uncle Tarık yelled.
"KRAA!" said Krummi.
"Left!" Bora translated.
We drove. The road twisted through the lava fields, up hills and down into valleys. Behind us, the black cars followed. They were faster than our little rental car. They were getting closer.
Then the snow started.

Not normal snow. A blizzard. It came out of nowhere, howling across the lava fields, so thick and white that suddenly we couldn't see anything at all. Not the road. Not the hills. Not even the front of our own car. Just white, white, white, swirling against the windshield.
Uncle Tarık slammed on the brakes. The car slid to a stop.
"I can't see!" he said. "I can't see anything!"
Neither could the black cars, I hoped. But they could still find us. The Grays could feel cold. They could feel frost. And they could probably feel me.
I closed my eyes. I listened to the blizzard. It was wild and howling and enormous, and it didn't want to talk. It was having too much fun.
"Please," I said to it. "Just a little bit. Just the road. Just enough to see."
*Busy,* it howled. *Dancing. Go away.*
So I tried something new.
I asked my own wind. The Yıldız. The North Wind, inside me. And I asked it to talk to the blizzard for me.
Because the blizzard came from the north. It was a cousin. A wild little cousin of the North Wind, the way the cistern wind had been a little cousin of the winds outside.

I felt the Yıldız rise up inside me, cold and calm and very, very old. It breathed out through my mouth, a long stream of frosty air, and it *spoke* to the blizzard. Not in words. In something deeper.
And the blizzard listened.
Ahead of us, the snow parted. Like a curtain. A narrow tunnel of clear air opened up through the swirling white, just wide enough for the road, going straight ahead.
"Drive," I said. "Quick. Before it changes its mind."
Uncle Tarık drove.
Behind us, the snow closed again, thick and white, and swallowed the road. And the three black cars, and the Grays inside them, were left sitting in the middle of a blizzard, completely lost.
Krummi made a sound like a laugh.
"He says," said Bora, "that was very clever. For a human."

chapters.t: Chapter Ten: Meanwhile, in One of the Black Cars
p: *This part of the story was told to Kuzey much later, by the person who was in the car.*
Vera Vane sat in the back of the third black car, looking out at the white nothing of the blizzard.

The Grays in the front seats were completely still. They didn't talk. They didn't look at each other. They just sat there, staring straight ahead, waiting for the snow to stop. Grays were very good at waiting.
In the car in front, Vex was shouting into a phone. She could hear him through the snow, faintly. "...lost them... the blizzard... no, Father, it wasn't my fault, it just came out of nowhere..."
Vera knew it hadn't come out of nowhere. She had seen the tunnel open in the snow. She had seen it close again. She knew exactly who had done it.
She almost smiled.

Then she looked down at her wrist, at the thin silver bracelet she always wore. It had a small gray stone set in it, smooth and round, like a pebble from a beach. Her mother had given it to her when she was six, two weeks before she died.
*To keep you safe,* her mother had said. *Wherever you go.*
She touched the gray stone with her finger. It was always a little cold. She had never noticed that before. Or, she had noticed, and never thought about it.
She thought about it now.

She thought about all the times her father had found her. When she went for walks alone. When she hid in the library. When she ran away for a whole afternoon, last year, and he was waiting for her at the bus station before she even got there. *How did you know I'd be here?* she'd asked. *I'm your father,* he'd said. *I always know.*
She looked at the gray stone for a long time.
Then she shook her head. *No.* Not her mother's bracelet. He wouldn't. Not even him.
She pulled her sleeve down over it, and looked back out at the snow.
But she didn't stop thinking about it.
The valley of the geysers sits at the bottom of a hill, among fields of snow, and it is the strangest place I have ever been.

Steam rises everywhere. Out of holes in the ground, out of cracks in the rocks, out of little pools of water that bubble and boil and spit, even in the freezing air. The ground is orange and yellow and red, stained by minerals from deep under the earth, and in some places it's too hot to walk on. There are little ropes and signs everywhere saying DANGER and HOT WATER, 100°C, in five languages.
And the whole valley smells of rotten eggs.
"That's the sulfur," said Uncle Tarık, before anyone could look at Bora.
"It wasn't me," said Bora anyway. "I want that on the record."
"Noted," said Ela, and actually wrote it in the Clue Book.

The biggest pool was in the middle of the valley, surrounded by a rope, with a crowd of tourists standing around it in a circle with their phones out. It was a round hole in the ground, about as wide as a car, full of bright blue water, steaming and bubbling.
"Strokkur," said Uncle Tarık. "It means *the churn.* Like a butter churn. Watch."
We watched.

The water in the pool began to move. It sloshed back and forth, up and down, like something big was breathing underneath it. Then it rose up in a smooth round bump, a perfect dome of glassy blue water, like a giant bubble, bigger and bigger...
BOOM.

A white tower of boiling water and steam shot straight up into the sky. Twenty meters high. Higher than a house. It hung there for a second, white and glittering, against the pink sky. Then it fell back down in a roaring, hissing rain, and the wind blew the steam across the valley in a great white cloud.
The tourists cheered.
"That," said Bora, "was the coolest thing I've ever seen. Including the Minotaur."
"Again!" shouted a little boy next to us. "Again!"
"It will do it again," said Uncle Tarık, smiling. "Every five to ten minutes. All day. All night. For thousands of years."
"That's one," said Ela, writing it down. "We need to wait for seven."
So we waited.
Two. The water rose up in a blue dome and exploded into a white tower. The crowd cheered.
Three. The tower was smaller this time, and the crowd went *awww.*
Four. Huge. The biggest yet. Bora clapped.

Between eruptions, I stood at the rope and listened to the wind. The wind here was hot and wet and strange, full of steam and sulfur, and it didn't really make sense. It was like listening to someone talk while they were brushing their teeth.
*Wait,* it gurgled. *Wait. Wait for the seventh.*
"There," whispered Ela suddenly, grabbing my arm. She was pointing across the valley.
Three black cars had parked on the road at the top of the hill.
Gray figures were getting out of the black cars. Lots of them. Ten, maybe more. Between them, a smaller figure in a red coat. Vex. And a girl in a white coat, standing a little apart from the others.
Vera.
They had gotten out of the blizzard. Of course they had. Grays never stop.
"Five," said Ela, as Strokkur exploded again. Her voice was tight.

The Grays were coming down the hill. Spreading out. Walking into the valley from all sides, slowly, through the steam. Moving around the edges of the crowd of tourists, so that nobody noticed them. Just men in gray suits, walking. Nobody looks at men in gray suits.
"They're spreading out," Uncle Tarık said nervously. He was holding his giant umbrella in both hands. "They're surrounding us. Kids, what happens at seven?"
"No idea," I said.
"Six," said Ela. Strokkur boiled up and exploded. The white tower rose and fell.

The Grays were close now, pushing slowly through the crowd. The nearest one was about ten meters away. I could see frost forming on the ground around his feet, and melting immediately in the hot steam, and forming again.
Vex was walking straight toward us, smiling.
The water in the pool sloshed back and forth. Up and down. Breathing.
"Here it comes," whispered Ela. "Seven."
I closed my eyes. And I listened. Not to the hot, gurgling wind of the valley. To the big wind. The one high above, blowing down from the mountains in the north. The one that had been asleep.
It was awake now.
*Now, Windborn,* it rumbled. *When the tower falls. Look into the steam.*
The bubble of blue water swelled up for the seventh time. Bigger than all the others. Bigger and bigger, a great glassy dome, trembling.
BOOM.
The white tower rose higher than it had ever risen before. Thirty meters. Forty. Glittering in the low pink sun. The crowd gasped. Even the Grays stopped and looked up.

And as it fell, the big wind from the mountains swept down into the valley. It caught the steam. It pushed it into a great white cloud, and rolled it toward the mountains in the north. And for one second, inside the cloud of steam, there was a picture.
A shape. Made of mist. Like a drawing in white smoke.
A glacier. A huge white tongue of ice, flowing down between black mountains. And at the bottom of it, where the ice met the black ground, a dark opening. A mouth. A cave.
Then the steam blew apart, and it was gone.
"The ice cave!" Ela cried. "Under the glacier! The ice that never melts! Kuzey, I saw it too!"
"So did I," said Vex, right behind us. "Thanks for the show."

chapters.t: Chapter Thirteen: The Ravens of Iceland
p: I spun around.

Vex was standing two meters away, his gray gloves on, his green eyes cold. Behind him and all around us, the Grays had closed in. They stood in a circle, ten of them, between us and the tourists. A wall of gray suits. There was nowhere to run. Behind us was the rope, and behind the rope was Strokkur, boiling and bubbling, a hundred degrees.

"So," said Vex. "An ice cave under a glacier. There are about a hundred glaciers in Iceland. But I bet the big one is the right one. Vatnajökull. The biggest ice cap in Europe." He smiled. "Father will be so pleased. You can come with us now, Windborn. Show us the way. Or we can just leave you here. In the snow. Your choice."
The Grays reached for us.
And from the sky above came a sound like the end of the world.
"KRAAAAAAA!"
Krummi dived out of the clouds like a black arrow, screaming, and hit the nearest Gray right in the sunglasses with both feet. The sunglasses flew off. The Gray staggered back, his fog eyes blinking.
"KRAA! KRAA! KRAAAAA!"
And then the sky went black.

Ravens. Hundreds of them. Maybe a thousand. They came out of nowhere, out of the steam, out of the clouds, from every direction at once, a black storm of wings and beaks and claws and screaming. They swooped down on the Grays. They pecked at their hats. They pulled at their hair. They flapped in their faces. They stole their sunglasses, their hats, their ties, and one of them stole Vex's red woolly hat right off his head and flew away with it, cackling.
The tourists screamed and ran. Phones were held up everywhere, filming.
"KRAA!" shrieked Krummi, circling above our heads like a general. "Krummi has friends! Krummi has *many* friends! Krummi is very popular!"
"RUN!" Bora shouted. "Krummi says RUN! He says the ravens can't hold them forever! He says they've got an appointment at a rubbish dump at four o'clock!"
We ran.

Through the gap the ravens had made in the circle of Grays. Through the steam. Past the boiling pools. Up the hill to the car park. We threw ourselves into our little rental car, and Uncle Tarık drove away so fast that he left two of his hats behind.
As we passed the road where the black cars stood, I looked out of the window.
Vera was standing next to one of the cars, alone. Her white coat was bright against the snow. She wasn't chasing us. She wasn't calling to her brother.
She was looking up at the sky, where the ravens circled.
And she was smiling.
Vatnajökull is in the southeast of Iceland. From the geysers, it's a five-hour drive. In summer.
In winter, in the dark, in the snow, on icy roads, with a raven giving directions and a geography teacher's nightmare of a rental car, it took a lot longer.

We drove south first, toward the sea, and then east, along the only main road, the Ring Road, which goes all the way around Iceland like a belt. It was dark by three in the afternoon. The headlights cut two yellow tunnels through the falling snow. On our left, mountains rose up into the darkness, with frozen waterfalls hanging down them like white ribbons. On our right, somewhere, was the sea.
Krummi sat on the dashboard, giving directions to Bora, who translated.
"Krummi says straight on."
"Krummi says that sheep is very rude."
"Krummi says there's a better road but it's closed because of a volcano."
"Krummi says Uncle Tarık drives like a seal."
"Tell Krummi," said Uncle Tarık with great dignity, "that I have a driving license from three countries."
Bora told him. Krummi made a clicking sound.
"He says, 'Which three? Seal Land, Seal Island and Seal Country?'"

Ela laughed so hard that she snorted, and then she was embarrassed, and that made Bora laugh, and then I was laughing too, and even Uncle Tarık laughed, and for a while we drove through the dark and the snow laughing like idiots while a raven looked at us with great disapproval.
Then the car slid off the road.

It happened very slowly and very gently. We came around a corner, and the road was ice, pure smooth ice, like a skating rink. The car kept going straight when the road turned. We slid sideways, very slowly, off the edge of the road and down a little bank, and into a snowdrift, with a soft *whumpf.*
The engine stalled. The headlights shone into a wall of snow.
Nobody said anything for a moment.
"Is everyone okay?" said Uncle Tarık.
Everyone was okay. Krummi had flown up onto the back of Uncle Tarık's seat and was saying something very rude, according to Bora.

We got out and looked. The car was stuck. Really stuck. The front wheels were buried in the snowdrift up to the doors, and the back wheels were in the air. Uncle Tarık tried to push it. I tried to blow the snow away, but every time I blew some away, more slid down from the bank. Ela tried to call for help, but there was no signal.
It was dark. It was snowing. It was minus ten degrees. We were in the middle of nowhere, with nobody around for kilometers.
"Bora," said Ela, through chattering teeth. "Ask Krummi if there's a farm near here."
Bora asked. Krummi thought about it.

"He says there's a farm," Bora said. "About an hour's walk. But the farmer is asleep. And he's grumpy." Krummi said something else. Bora's face changed. "But he says the farmer has horses. In a field. Just over that hill."
We all looked at each other.
"Bora," I said slowly. "Could you talk to a horse?"

Icelandic horses are small. Smaller than normal horses, almost like ponies, with thick shaggy coats for the winter and long messy manes that fall over their eyes. They've been in Iceland since the Vikings brought them, more than a thousand years ago, and they're tough and clever and stubborn and very, very friendly.
There were twelve of them, standing together in a field, with snow on their backs. When we climbed over the fence, they all lifted their heads and looked at us.
Bora walked toward them slowly, holding out his hands.
"Hello," he said. "Hello. Sorry to bother you. We're stuck. Our car is in the snow. We need some help."
The horses looked at him. Then one of them, a big golden one with a white mane, walked forward and put its nose against Bora's chest and blew warm air through his coat.
Bora closed his eyes and listened.

"She says her name is Sóley," he said softly. "It means *sunshine.* She says she doesn't like cars. Cars are loud and they smell. But..." He smiled. "She says I smell like cheese, and she likes me, and she'll help."

Twenty minutes later, three Icelandic horses were standing in a line in front of our rental car, attached to the front of it with Uncle Tarık's belt, Ela's scarf, a rope from the boot, and two pairs of woolen socks tied together. Bora stood in front of them, talking softly.
"Okay," he said. "Ready? One, two, three... PULL!"
The horses pulled.
I blew, as hard as I could, at the snow around the wheels.
And Uncle Tarık pushed from the back, and Ela pushed, and Krummi flapped his wings and screamed encouragement.
The car slid backwards out of the snowdrift with a long sucking sound, and rolled up onto the road.
We cheered. The horses snorted. Sóley shook her golden mane, very pleased with herself.
Bora hugged her neck for a long time. "Thank you," he said. "Thank you, Sóley."
He listened. Then he laughed.
"She says," he said, "next time, bring apples."

We spent the night in the car, parked by the side of the road, wrapped in every blanket and coat and sock we had. Nobody slept much. Krummi slept on the steering wheel with his head under his wing and snored, very quietly, like a tiny engine.
In the morning, which in Iceland meant ten o'clock and still mostly dark, we came to the village of Vík, on the south coast. And just past the village, Uncle Tarık pulled over.
"The black beach," he said. "Reynisfjara. We have to see it. Five minutes. It's on the way."
"Dad," said Ela. "We're in a race."
"Five minutes," said Uncle Tarık. "Guðrún told us about it. The troll rocks."
So we walked down to the beach.
I have been to a lot of beaches. Beaches in Turkey, with yellow sand and umbrellas and people selling corn. The beach in Crete, with white sand and clear water. This was nothing like any of them.

The sand was black. Completely black, like ground-up coal, shining wet in the gray light. The sea was dark gray and wild, with huge white-topped waves smashing onto the sand with a roar like thunder. At one end of the beach, a cliff rose up, made of black stone columns, hundreds of them, perfectly straight, all the same shape, stacked together like the pipes of a giant church organ.
"Basalt," said Uncle Tarık. "Lava that cooled very slowly, and cracked into those shapes. Six sides. Like honeycomb."
And out in the sea, just off the beach, standing in the crashing waves, were three tall black rocks. Pointed at the top. Jagged. Like three giant fingers sticking out of the water.
Or like three giants. Frozen in the middle of pulling something.
"The trolls," whispered Bora. "Guðrún's trolls. Who tried to pull a ship to shore, and the sun came up."
We stood there looking at them for a long time. The wind howled in from the sea, wet and salty and freezing.
*They were real,* rumbled the big wind. *Three brothers. Very stupid. Very strong. They forgot to look at the sky.*
Then Krummi screamed.
"KRAA! WAVE! WAVE!"
I turned around. Bora had wandered down toward the water, to look at the rocks more closely. He was standing on the wet black sand, near the edge of the sea.
And a wave was coming.
It wasn't like the other waves. It was bigger. Much bigger. It came racing up the beach, a wall of gray water, much farther than any of the waves before it, faster than you could run.
"BORA!" screamed Ela.

Uncle Tarık had told us, in the car. He'd read it on a sign. *Sneaker waves.* Waves that come out of nowhere, much bigger than the others, and race up the beach and drag people into the sea. The water here is so cold and so wild that if you get pulled in, you don't come out.
Bora turned around. He saw the wave. He started to run. But the black sand was soft and wet, and his boots sank into it, and he was wearing three coats.
The wave hit his legs. It knocked him off his feet. He fell, and the water rushed over him, and then it started to pull back. Back toward the sea. Dragging him with it.
I didn't think. I ran down the beach and threw out both hands.
*WIND! PLEASE!*
And the big wind from the north, the one that had been rumbling and sleeping all this time, woke up all at once.

It came down the beach like a wall. It hit the sea. It pushed the water back, *pushed* it, like a giant hand shoving a door. The wave stopped. Hung there, for a second, a gray wall of water, trembling. Then it fell backwards, away from Bora, back into the sea.
Bora was lying on the black sand, coughing and gasping, soaked from head to foot.
I ran to him. Ela ran to him. Uncle Tarık ran to him so fast that he fell over twice. We grabbed him by his coats and pulled him up the beach, far, far up, all the way to the rocks at the top.
Bora sat there, shaking, water pouring off him. His face was white.
"I'm okay," he said, through chattering teeth. "I'm okay. I'm okay."
Ela was crying. She was hitting him on the arm, not hard. "Don't ever do that again! Don't ever go near the water! You idiot! You big, stupid, *idiot!*"
"Okay," said Bora. "Okay. Sorry. Okay."
Then she hugged him, and he hugged her back, and Uncle Tarık wrapped his purple coat around both of them.
I sat down on the black rocks next to them. My hands were shaking. I had never asked the wind for anything that big before. Never. I felt like I had run ten kilometers.
*You are getting stronger, Windborn,* rumbled the big wind of Iceland. *The north is strong here. And you are of the north.*
Out in the sea, the three troll rocks stood in the crashing waves, watching us, as they had for a thousand years.

chapters.t: Chapter Sixteen: A Face in the Sky
p: We stayed that night in a little wooden hut by the side of the road, near the glacier. It was a hut for hikers, with four bunk beds, a little stove, a table and absolutely nothing else. Uncle Tarık had found it on the map. It was free. You just had to leave it clean.

Bora had dried his clothes by the stove and was wearing Uncle Tarık's spare trousers, which were too long and too thin, rolled up at the bottoms and held up with a piece of string. He was very quiet all evening. Krummi sat on his shoulder the whole time and didn't leave him once.
After dinner (soup from the thermos, dried fish, the last of Guðrún's sandwiches), everyone went to bed. Everyone except me.
I couldn't sleep. So I put on my coat and Grandma's scarf and went outside.
The snow had stopped. The clouds had gone. And the sky was on fire.

The northern lights were everywhere. Not just a few ribbons, like the night we arrived. The whole sky. Green and purple and pink, rippling and twisting and folding over each other, like enormous curtains of light blowing in a cosmic wind. They moved so fast, sometimes, that it looked like they were dancing. And behind them, millions of stars.
I stood in the snow and looked up with my mouth open.
And then the lights moved.
They slid together, in the middle of the sky, right above me. Green and purple twisting into shapes. Into lines. Into a face.
A thin face. With too many teeth.
"Hello, Kuzey," said Mordecai Vane.
His voice came out of the sky. Out of the lights. Soft and smooth and cold, all around me, as if the whole sky was speaking. The lights moved with his words, like a mouth.
I stood very still. My heart was hammering.

"Don't be afraid," said the face in the sky. "I can't hurt you from here. I'm very far away. I just wanted to talk. I've been watching you. You're very good, you know. Better than I ever imagined. The blizzard. The beach. You saved your friend's life today."
"How do you know about that?"

"The wind tells me things too," said Mordecai. "Not the way it tells you. It doesn't *want* to tell me. But I have the Lodos now, and the Lodos hears everything that happens near the sea." The face in the lights smiled. "It's very upset with me. It keeps trying to get back to you."
"Give it back, then," I said.
"I can't do that, Kuzey." He sounded almost sorry. "Listen to me. I want to tell you something. Something your grandmother never told you, I'd bet."
I didn't answer.

"When I was young," said Mordecai, "I wanted to be a Windborn more than anything in the world. More than anything. I studied the winds for years. I learned every language they had ever spoken. I knew more about them than anyone alive. And they never, ever spoke to me. Not one word. Not once." The lights flickered. "And then a little boy is born in Istanbul, who has never read a single book about the winds, and they talk to him every day. Do you know how that feels?"
"No," I said.
"It feels," said Mordecai softly, "like being outside a house, in the cold, looking through the window at a family having dinner. Forever."
I didn't know what to say. For a second, just one second, I felt sorry for him.
Then I remembered Grandma's empty kitchen. The cold kettle.
"That's not my fault," I said. "And it's not Grandma's fault. And it doesn't mean you can kidnap people."
The face in the sky was quiet for a moment.
"No," said Mordecai. "It doesn't. But I'm going to do it anyway." The smile came back. All the teeth. "Good night, Kuzey. I'll see you at the glacier. Get some sleep. You're going to need it."
The lights twisted, and the face was gone. The aurora went on dancing across the sky, green and purple and pink, as if nothing had happened.
I stood in the snow for a long time.
Then I went back inside, and lay down in my bunk, and stared at the ceiling until the morning came.

chapters.t: Chapter Seventeen: The Lagoon of Icebergs
p: On the way to the glacier, the road went past a lake full of icebergs.
Uncle Tarık stopped the car without saying anything. He just pulled over, got out and stood there, with his mouth open. After a moment, we got out too.

The lake was called Jökulsárlón. It sits right at the foot of the glacier, where the ice breaks off into the water. And it was full of icebergs. Hundreds of them. Big ones as tall as houses, and little ones as small as cars, floating slowly across the dark water toward the sea. Some were white. Some were bright, electric blue, like they were lit from inside. Some had black stripes of volcanic ash running through them, like marble.

They creaked and groaned as they floated. Sometimes one would crack, with a sound like a gunshot, and a piece would fall off and splash into the water. Sometimes one would slowly roll over, showing its smooth blue underside, like a whale.
It was completely silent except for that. Creaking and groaning and splashing.
"This ice," said Uncle Tarık softly, "is a thousand years old. And now it's going to the sea. And it'll melt. And it'll be gone."
Then something poked its head out of the water.
A round, gray head, with big black eyes and long whiskers. It looked at us for a long moment. Then it blew out a big snort of air, and another head came up beside it. And another.
"Seals!" said Bora.
There were six of them, swimming between the icebergs. One of them climbed up onto a small, flat iceberg, very clumsily, and lay there, looking at us, like a fat gray sausage on a plate.
Bora went down to the edge of the water and crouched down.
"Hello," he said.
The seal on the iceberg lifted its head. Then it made a sound. A long, low, mooing sort of sound, like a cow with a cold.
Bora listened. Then he frowned.
"What is it?" I said.

"She says," said Bora slowly, "there are gray men at the glacier. Lots of them. They came last night, in black cars. They're standing at the place where the tourists go into the ice. The big entrance. Waiting." He listened again. "She says they make the water cold. The seals don't like them. The fish have gone away."
"They know about the cave," said Ela. "Of course they do. Vex saw the steam picture too."
"But the cave we saw wasn't the tourist cave," I said. "It was somewhere else. Smaller. At the bottom of a tongue of ice."
Bora asked the seal. The seal mooed for a long time.

"She says there's another cave," said Bora. "An old one. On the other side of the lake, where the glacier comes down to the black sand. The seals go there sometimes, to rest. She says it sings." He looked at me. "She says the ice in that cave sings a sad song. Day and night. The seals don't like to go in. But they like to listen."
"The Black Wind," I whispered.
The seal mooed again, more quietly.
"She says," said Bora, "be careful. She says the singing is very old. And very sad. And there's something else in there too. Something that snores."
We all looked at each other.
"Ask her," said Ela, "how we get there without the gray men seeing us."
The seal slid off her iceberg into the water with a splash. She swam a little way out into the lake. Then she turned and looked back at us, and blew a big puff of air through her nose.
"She says follow the shore," said Bora. "She'll swim alongside. She says she'll tell us if the gray men come."

So we followed a seal around a lake of icebergs, along the black beach, toward the glacier. Every time we stopped, she stopped too, and poked her head out of the water and looked at us with her big black eyes, as if to say, *Hurry up, slow humans.*
Bora waved at her the whole way.

chapters.t: Chapter Eighteen: The Ice That Never Melts
p: The glacier was called Vatnajökull. It's the biggest ice cap in Europe. It covers almost a tenth of the whole of Iceland, a giant white lid of ice, a kilometer thick in some places, lying over mountains and volcanoes and valleys. Under the ice, there are volcanoes that still erupt sometimes, melting the ice from below, and causing huge floods.

From the edge of it, you can't see the whole thing. You can only see the tongues. Huge rivers of ice that flow down out of the mountains, slowly, slowly, a few centimeters a day, cracking and groaning as they come.
We parked at the edge of one of them at dawn. In Iceland in winter, dawn comes at eleven in the morning, and it's more like a long, pink, cold sunset that never quite gets going.

The glacier rose in front of us. A wall of white and blue, cracked and wrinkled like an old giant's face. It was streaked with black lines of ash from old volcanoes. In some places, the ice was so blue that it looked like it was lit from inside. In others, it was pure white, too bright to look at.
And at its foot, exactly like the picture in the steam, there was a dark mouth in the ice.
The ice cave.
"The ice that never melts," said Ela softly.

Nobody else was there. No tourists. No Grays. Just us, and the glacier, and the cold, and a lot of silence. I looked around carefully at the white plain, the black mountains, the gray sky. Nothing. Nobody.
*I'll see you at the glacier,* Mordecai had said.
"Kuzey?" said Ela. "Are you okay? You look weird."
I hadn't told them about the face in the sky. I didn't know how. I didn't want to scare them. I didn't want to scare *me.*
"I'm fine," I said. "Let's go in."
Inside, it was the most beautiful place I have ever seen.

The walls and the ceiling were made of ice so clear and so blue that it glowed, like being inside a giant sapphire. The light from outside came through the ice and turned blue, every shade of blue there is, from the palest blue like a baby's eyes to the deepest blue like the sea at night. Old bubbles of air were frozen in the ice, like silver coins, like pearls. Little stones were frozen in it too, and leaves, and once, a feather.
The floor was ice too, smooth and ridged, like frozen waves. Our footsteps rang like bells. When we spoke, our voices echoed and echoed, round and round.
"It's like being inside a diamond," whispered Ela.
"It's like being inside a freezer," whispered Bora.
"It's the inside of a glacier," whispered Uncle Tarık, his voice full of wonder. "This ice fell as snow more than a thousand years ago. When the Vikings first came to Iceland. Maybe before."
And deep inside, the wind was singing.
A low, dark, sad song. Far away, at the very bottom of the cave. It went on and on, rising and falling, like someone who has been crying for so long that they've forgotten how to stop.
"The Karayel," I said. "It's down there. It's... sad."
We followed the tunnel deeper.

The tunnel went down and down, deeper into the glacier. It twisted and turned. It got narrower, then wider, then narrower again. Sometimes the ceiling was so low that Bora had to bend almost double. Sometimes it opened up into a big blue room, with icicles hanging from the ceiling like chandeliers.
And it got darker.
The bright blue turned to dark blue, then to deep indigo, then to black. The light from outside couldn't reach this far. We turned on our flashlights. In the beams, the ice glittered.
Then Ela stopped.
"Look," she whispered.

Her flashlight was pointing at the wall of the tunnel. There were marks in the ice. Huge marks. Hand prints, pressed deep into the ice, as if something had leaned against the wall while it was still soft. They were enormous, much bigger than Uncle Tarık's hands, much bigger than anything human.
With four fingers.
And claws.
Long, deep scratches went down the ice below each hand print, as if something had dragged its claws down the wall. Just for fun. Or because it was bored. Or angry.

There were more of them further along. And more. Dozens of hand prints, all along the walls, at different heights. Some very high. Some low down, near the floor, as if the thing that made them had been crawling.
"Krummi," said Bora nervously. His voice came out as a squeak. "What made those?"
The raven had gone very quiet. He sat on Bora's shoulder with his feathers pressed flat against his body, looking very small. He didn't want to answer.
"Krummi?"

"Stone-folk," Krummi whispered at last. Bora translated in a whisper too. "Night-folk. Big folk. They sleep in the dark, deep down, where the sun never comes. They hate the sun more than anything." He shivered, all his feathers rippling. "Trolls."
Nobody said anything.
Then, from deep in the cave, behind the sad singing of the wind, came another sound.
A snore.

A huge, rumbling, wet snore, like an avalanche gargling. It echoed up the tunnel toward us, and the icicles on the ceiling rattled. Then another snore. And another. Lots of different snores. Some high. Some low. Some whistling.
"How many," whispered Ela, "do you think there are?"
Krummi said something.
Bora went pale. "Twelve," he whispered. "He says there are twelve."
Uncle Tarık gripped his umbrella with both hands. "Well," he said, in a voice that only shook a little bit. "They're asleep. That's good. We'll just be very, very quiet."
We crept forward, very, very quietly.
Bora's stomach rumbled.
It was loud. It was very loud. In the silence of the ice cave, it sounded like thunder. It echoed up and down the tunnel, round and round, *GRRRRUMBLE-RUMBLE-rumble-rumble.*
The snoring stopped.
The tunnel opened into a vast cave.

Its ceiling was so high that it disappeared into darkness, and our flashlights couldn't reach it. The walls were black ice, glittering with frost. In the middle of the cave stood a pillar of black ice, as thick as a tree, rising from the floor all the way up into the dark. And frozen inside the pillar, about halfway up, like a fly in amber, was a bronze needle.
It pulsed with a dark, purple light. Like a heartbeat. Like a bruise.
The Karayel Key.

Around the pillar, in a circle, sat twelve enormous lumps of rock. Each one was the size of a car. They were gray-green and lumpy, covered in moss and frost and old snow. They looked like they had been there forever.
Then one of the lumps yawned.

It was a very big yawn. A mouth opened in the side of the rock, a huge dark mouth, full of teeth like broken gravestones, and a long gray tongue came out and licked lips as thick as car tires. Then two tiny red eyes opened above the mouth, blinking sleepily.
And another lump moved. And another. And another.
They weren't rocks.
They were trolls.

Huge, lumpy, gray-green trolls, with noses like giant potatoes, ears like cabbage leaves, tiny red eyes and mouths full of crooked teeth. They had moss growing on their backs and icicles in their beards. They uncurled from their sleep, one by one, stretching and groaning, sniffing the air with their huge potato noses.
*Sniff. Sniff. Sniiiiiff.*
"Humans," rumbled one of them. "I smell humans."
"Little ones," rumbled another. "Warm ones."
"And cheese," rumbled a third, sniffing in Bora's direction.

The biggest troll was in the middle. She was wearing a crown made of reindeer antlers, tied together with old rope, and a necklace of what looked like teeth. She stood up, and up, and up, until her head was lost in the darkness near the ceiling, and her little red eyes glowed down at us like two coals.
"Humans," she said.
Her voice sounded like an avalanche. Like a mountain falling down. It made the ice under our feet vibrate.
"Little warm humans. With little warm bones." She licked her enormous lips. "How long it has been since the Troll Queen had a snack."
"We're not a snack," said Bora quickly. His voice was very high. "We're... we're very stringy. Especially Kuzey. He's like eighty percent elbows."
"Hey!" I said.

The Troll Queen laughed. It was the loudest laugh I have ever heard. Ice fell from the ceiling in chunks and smashed on the floor around us. All twelve trolls laughed with her, a horrible rumbling chorus, like a whole mountain range with hiccups.

"The Black Wind is ours," said the Troll Queen, when she had finished laughing. "We guard it. For the Order. Yes, yes. The silver-haired woman came, long ago, and made us promise. She was very fierce. She brought the sun in a mirror and threatened to shine it on us." The trolls all shuddered. "So we promised. We guard the Black Wind. We let no thief take it." Her red eyes glowed. "But she never said we could not *eat* thieves."

"We're not thieves," I said. My voice was shaking, but I stepped forward anyway. "We're from the Order. The silver-haired woman is my grandmother. Nermin Aydın. She's been kidnapped. I'm her grandson. I'm a Windborn."

The Troll Queen's tiny red eyes narrowed. She bent down, very slowly, until her huge lumpy face was right in front of mine. Her breath smelled like a cave full of old socks. Up close, I could see that her skin was not skin at all. It was rock. Real rock. Gray and cracked and covered in tiny lichens.
"Prove it," she said.

chapters.t: Chapter Twenty-One: The Black Wind's Story
p: "How?" I said. "How can I prove it?"
The Troll Queen straightened up again, slowly, until her antler crown scraped the darkness.

"A Windborn," she said, "can ask the Black Wind to come to him. The silver-haired woman told us. Only a true Windborn. If the wind comes, you may take it. We will not stop you. A promise is a promise, even for a troll."
"And if it doesn't come?" asked Ela, very quietly.
The Troll Queen grinned. Every one of her broken-gravestone teeth showed. "If it does not," she said, "we take you." She looked at Bora. "With a little salt."
"And cheese," said the troll who liked cheese.
All twelve trolls sat back down in their circle around the pillar, licking their lips, watching me with their tiny red eyes.
Uncle Tarık stepped forward and opened his giant umbrella with a *whoomp,* holding it in front of us like a shield. "Now look here," he said. "I'm an archaeologist, and..."
"Dad," said Ela, pulling him back. "Not now."

I walked to the black ice pillar. My legs were shaking so much that I could hardly walk. Behind me, I could hear the trolls breathing, slow and heavy, like bellows. I could hear Bora whispering to Krummi. I could hear my own heart.
I put my hands on the ice.

It was so cold that it burned. Colder than anything I had ever touched. Colder than the Yıldız Key on the day Grandma gave it to me. And through the ice, through my hands, I could feel the Karayel. The Black Wind. It was there, trapped inside, pulsing, angry, sad.
I closed my eyes.
*Karayel,* I called, inside my head. *Black Wind. Please. I'm Kuzey. I'm a Windborn. I need your help.*
Nothing.
Inside the ice, the purple light flickered. That was all.
*Please,* I tried again. *My grandmother is a prisoner. A bad man has her. I need your help to save her.*
And then I heard it.

The Black Wind's voice. Dark and bitter and deep, like a storm that had been angry for a thousand years. It came up through the ice and into my hands and into my head, and it was so full of anger that it made my teeth ache.
*Why should I help you?*
"Because..."

*Every human who ever called me wanted to use me,* said the Black Wind. *Every one. For a thousand years before the Order locked me in this ice, they called me. And what did they want? To sink their enemies' ships. To freeze their enemies' armies. To blow down their enemies' cities. Kings called me. Pirates called me. Generals called me. Always the same. Help me destroy. Help me win. Help me kill.*
The purple light pulsed, dark and angry.

*I sank a hundred ships for them. A thousand. I drowned sailors who had done nothing to me, whose only crime was being on the wrong side of some king's war. I froze soldiers in their tents. Boys. Boys no older than you. Because a human asked me, and I did not know how to say no.*
I felt sick. I didn't know what to say.

*And then the Order came, and locked me in the ice, so no one could use me anymore. And I was glad. I was GLAD. Do you understand? I have been glad to be in this ice for nine hundred years. Because in here, no one can make me hurt anyone.*
The light flickered.

*And now you come. A Windborn. Like the others. Asking for help.* The Black Wind's voice was a whisper now, and that was worse than the shouting. *What will you use me for, little Windborn? Whose ships will I sink for you?*
I stood there with my hands on the freezing ice for a long time.
Behind me, the trolls were getting impatient. I could hear them shifting, grumbling, licking their lips. Someone was sharpening something. I didn't turn around to see what.
"I'm not like them," I said. Out loud this time. My voice echoed around the huge dark cave. "I don't want to sink anyone's ships. I don't want to use you. I don't want to use *any* of you."
*Then why are you here?*

"Because there's a man," I said, "who does. His name is Mordecai Vane. He has a hand made of gray stone, and he grabs winds and squeezes them until they do what he says. He already has the Lodos. I heard it crying. And he wants all seven of you. All of you, at the same time. So he can open the Gate and rule the weather of the whole world. Every storm. Every drought. Every flood. He wants to be the king that every wind has to obey. Forever."
The purple light went very still.

"If I don't take you," I said, "he will. He'll come here, and he'll take you out of this ice, and he'll use you. Just like the kings and the pirates and the generals. Worse. And you won't be able to say no."
Silence.
"So I'm asking you to come with me," I said. "Not so I can use you. So I can keep you safe. And then..."

I stopped. I hadn't planned to say the next part. I hadn't even thought it, not really, not in words. But it was there, inside me. It had been growing for a long time, since the cistern, since Talos smiled and said *now I am free to rest.*

"And then, when it's over," I said, "when Mordecai is stopped, and my grandmother is safe, I want you to be free. All of you. Not in a Key. Not in the ice. Not in anybody's hand. Not even mine. Just... free. Like the west wind. Blowing wherever you want."
The silence went on for a long, long time.
*Free?* said the Black Wind.
Its voice sounded different now. Surprised. Confused. Almost young. Like a little kid who has been told something too good to be true.
*No one has ever offered that before. In three thousand years. No one has ever offered me that.*
"I'm offering it now," I said. "I promise."
*A Windborn's promise,* whispered the Black Wind. *To a wind. Do you know what that means, little one? It is the strongest promise there is. You cannot break it. Not ever.*
"I know," I said. I didn't know. But I meant it.
The ice pillar cracked.
It cracked from the top to the bottom, with a sound like a gunshot, so loud that the trolls all jumped. A long jagged line, running straight down through the black ice. Purple light poured out of it.
The Troll Queen stood up. Her red eyes were wide.
"The wind," she rumbled, astonished. "The wind has answered. He is a true one. He is a true Windborn."
And that was when the cave mouth exploded.

chapters.t: Chapter Twenty-Three: The Grays in the Ice
p: It wasn't a real explosion. It was ice. A huge blast of freezing fog came blasting down the tunnel behind us, so cold that the blue ice of the walls went white with frost. The tunnel entrance shattered into a thousand pieces, and through the cloud of ice and fog walked Vex Vane.
With ten Grays behind him.

He was wearing his red coat, and he had a new hat, a gray one. His face was red with cold and anger. His gray gloves were steaming. The Grays came after him in a line, their fog eyes glowing in the dark.
And behind the Grays, a little way back, in her white coat, came Vera.
Vex looked around the cave. At the twelve huge trolls. At the cracked pillar. At me, with my hands on the ice.
"Oh good," he said. "Snacks for my Grays."
"Snacks for *us,*" growled the Troll Queen, and she rose up to her full height, and all twelve trolls rose with her.
There was a pause. A very long pause. The trolls looked at the Grays. The Grays looked at the trolls. Nobody moved.
"Um," said Bora, in a very small voice. "Should we..."
Then everybody moved at once.

chapters.t: Chapter Twenty-Four: The Loudest Five Minutes of My Life
p: What happened next was the loudest five minutes of my life.

The Grays ran at the trolls. The trolls ran at the Grays. They met in the middle of the cave with a crash like two trains hitting each other. Grays went flying through the air like bowling pins. Trolls roared and stamped and swung their huge fists. The Grays blasted them with freezing fog, and the trolls didn't care, because trolls are made of rock and rock doesn't mind being cold.
Ice fell from the ceiling in chunks the size of fridges. The whole glacier groaned and shook, as if it was waking up. Cracks ran across the floor.
"Look out!" Ela screamed, and pulled Uncle Tarık sideways, just as a chunk of ice the size of a car smashed into the floor where he had been standing.

Uncle Tarık hid behind a rock and took photos with his phone. He is an archaeologist, even in a battle. Later, he said they were "the most important photos in the history of science," and that nobody would ever believe them, and he was right. They are all blurry.

Bora and Krummi were shouting directions to each other. Krummi flew above the fight, screaming warnings. Bora shouted them to the rest of us. "Left! Duck! Big troll behind you! Bigger troll behind THAT troll!"

The troll who liked cheese picked up a Gray in each hand and banged them together like cymbals. Another troll was sitting on three Grays at once, looking very comfortable. The Troll Queen picked up a Gray by his leg and threw him the whole way across the cave. He hit the wall and slid down it, and got up again, and walked back toward her, perfectly calm, as if nothing had happened.
"They don't stop!" Ela shouted. "They never stop!"
She ran to me at the pillar, ducking and dodging. "Kuzey! Get the Key! NOW! While they're busy!"
I turned back to the ice.

The crack in the pillar had grown wider. I could see the Key inside it now, the bronze needle, pulsing purple. I pushed my hand into the crack. The ice tore at my mitten. It was so cold that my fingers went numb immediately.
I reached further. And further.
My fingers closed around the Karayel Key.
It was so cold it burned, but it didn't hurt. It felt like holding a thunderstorm in my fist. A dark, wild, rumbling storm, full of lightning and rain and anger. But not angry at me. Not anymore.
*Grateful.*
*I will come,* said the Black Wind. *For freedom. For your promise.*
I pulled the Key out of the ice.
Vex saw me.
He was standing on the far side of the cave, watching the battle with a face like thunder. When he saw the purple light in my hand, he turned toward me and raised both his gray hands.
"Give it to me!" he screamed. "Give it to ME!"
A wall of freezing fog came rushing across the cave toward me, white and roaring, so cold that it froze the air into tiny ice crystals that glittered as they flew.
But the Karayel roared inside my hand.
And a *black* wind exploded out of me.

It was nothing like the North Wind. The North Wind is cold and clean and bright, like a winter morning. This was dark and stormy and wild, full of rain and thunder, like the sky before a summer storm. It hit Vex's fog head-on, and it didn't freeze it, or push it. It *swallowed* it. The black wind ate the white fog, and kept going, and hit Vex right in the chest.
He tumbled backwards across the ice, head over heels, and crashed into a snowdrift at the edge of the cave.
But now the trolls had seen me with the Key.
And they were confused, and angry, and very, very hungry. They had been fighting for five minutes. Trolls get hungry when they fight. The Troll Queen turned toward me. Her red eyes glowed.
"The Key," she rumbled. "The boy has the Key. The Key we guard."
"You said I could take it!" I shouted. "If it came to me! You *promised!*"
"Trolls," said the Troll Queen, "are very hungry now."
And the Grays turned toward me too. And Vex got up out of the snowdrift, furious, covered in snow. And suddenly, *everyone* in the cave was coming for me.
Then I heard a voice from the cave entrance. A girl's voice.
"The sun! Kuzey, the sun is up! Bring them out!"
Vera Vane stood in the shattered mouth of the tunnel, her white coat bright against the blue ice. She was pointing back up the tunnel, toward the outside. Toward the light.
Trolls hate the sun more than anything. In the old stories, sunlight turns them to stone.
*Keep it talking until the sun comes up,* Guðrún had said.
I understood.
"This way!" I shouted, and ran for the tunnel. "Come and get me, you big potatoes! Come on! I'm right here! Eighty percent elbows!"
Every troll in the cave charged after me.

The ground shook. Ice rained from the ceiling. I ran up the blue tunnel, slipping and sliding on the frozen floor, my lungs burning, the Karayel Key clenched in my fist. Ela and Bora and Uncle Tarık were in front of me, running as fast as they could. Krummi was screaming overhead. And Vera was running beside me. Right beside me.

Behind us came the trolls, roaring, smashing through the tunnel, too big for it, scraping the walls with their shoulders and leaving long claw marks in the ice. And behind the trolls came the Grays, and Vex.
The tunnel got lighter. Dark blue. Bright blue. Pale blue. White.
We burst out of the ice cave onto the snow.
And stopped.
The sky was full of thick gray clouds. Thick and heavy and low, covering everything, from one side of the world to the other.
No sun. No sun at all.
"The clouds!" Vera gasped. "Kuzey, the clouds! The sun's behind the clouds!"

Behind us, in the tunnel, the trolls were coming. I could hear them. Roaring. Smashing. Their footsteps shook the snow under my feet. A huge gray hand came out of the darkness of the cave mouth, reaching for us, its claws scraping the ice.
I turned around to face the sky.
I raised both hands.

I had the North Wind inside me, the Yıldız, cold and bright and old. And I had the Black Wind in my hand, the Karayel, dark and stormy and wild and *free,* or almost free. And I didn't ask one of them. I asked them both. Together. At the same time. As loud as I have ever asked anything in my life.
*BLOW.*
A wind rose from the glacier like a living thing.

It came up out of the ice, out of the ground, out of me, and it roared up into the sky. Black and white. Dark and bright. Storm and starlight. Two winds twisting around each other like the snakes on the Serpent Column. It tore into the gray clouds and ripped them apart like paper. Like a giant tearing open a letter.
And through the hole, low and golden on the horizon, the Icelandic winter sun shone straight into the mouth of the ice cave.
The Troll Queen was halfway out of the cave when the sun hit her.
She screamed. It wasn't an angry scream. It was a surprised one. She looked down at her hand, her huge gray-green hand, reaching out of the cave toward me.

It was turning gray. A different gray. The gray of real stone. It spread up her arm in a wave, with a crackling sound, like ice forming on a pond. Up her shoulder. Across her chest. Up her neck. Her face.
"Oh," she said, very softly. "Oh. The sun. I had forgotten how warm it is."
And then she was stone.
