A huge gray boulder in the shape of a troll, half in and half out of the mouth of the ice cave, one arm reaching out. Her antler crown was still on her head. And on her stone face, there was a very strange expression. Not angry. Not scared.
Almost peaceful.

Behind her, inside the tunnel, the sunlight poured in. And the other eleven trolls, crowding up the tunnel behind their queen, froze mid-run. One by one, with a crackling sound, they turned into lumpy gray boulders, all with very surprised faces. The troll who liked cheese was frozen with his mouth open and his hand stretched out, as if he was reaching for a sandwich.
The Grays behind them, trapped in the cave behind a wall of stone trolls, banged on the stone. We could hear them. *Bang. Bang. Bang.* Calm and steady, the way they did everything.
And then, from deep inside, Vex's voice, shouting with rage.
It was over.

We stood in the snow, breathing hard, in the golden light of the low winter sun. It shone across the glacier and turned everything gold and pink and blue. The ice sparkled like a million diamonds. It was the most beautiful light I have ever seen.
I opened my hand.

The Karayel Key glowed in my palm, purple and dark. Then, just like the Yıldız Key, it began to sink into my skin. It didn't hurt. It was cold and wild, and it slid into me like a fish slipping into water, and settled down inside me next to the North Wind.
I could feel them both. The Yıldız and the Karayel. Like two big dogs curling up together in front of a fire. Sniffing each other. Deciding to be friends.
*Thank you, Windborn,* said the Black Wind, from inside me. Its voice was much softer now. *For the sun. And the promise. Do not forget the promise.*
"I won't," I said.
I breathed out.

And my breath came out as a tiny black storm cloud. About the size of a football. It floated in front of my face, dark and puffy, with a tiny flash of lightning inside it. Then it rained a little bit. On my shoes.
Bora laughed so hard he fell over in the snow.

chapters.t: Chapter Twenty-Seven: The Girl in the White Coat
p: Vera Vane stood a few steps away, alone, her arms wrapped around herself.

She was shivering. Her white coat was torn at the shoulder, and there was ice in her hair. She was looking at the stone trolls in the cave mouth, and at the wall they made, with her brother and her father's Grays on the other side.
She looked very small, suddenly. Smaller than I had ever seen her.
"Why?" I asked her. "Why did you help us? Again?"
She didn't answer right away. When she did, her voice was very quiet.
"My father wasn't always like this," she said.

Ela had come up beside me. Bora, too, brushing the snow off his coat. Uncle Tarık, holding his umbrella. Krummi landed on Bora's shoulder. We all stood there in the snow, in the golden light, and listened.

"When I was little," said Vera, "he used to take us to see the sea. Me and Vex. Every Sunday. We'd stand on the beach, and he'd tell us stories about the winds. The north wind and the south wind, and the wind gods of Greece, and the winds of Persia, and the winds that Odysseus kept in a bag. He knew all the stories. He used to do all the voices." She smiled a little, but it was a sad smile. "He was really good at the voices."
She looked down at the snow.

"Then my mother got sick. And she died. And after that, he found an old book, about the Gate. And he put on the gray glove. And every year after that, he got colder." She swallowed. "He doesn't take us to the sea anymore. He doesn't tell stories. He doesn't do the voices. He just... looks at maps. And counts Keys. And gets colder."
She looked down at her hands. She wasn't wearing gloves. Just her bare hands, red with cold.

"Vex wants to be just like him," she said. "He thinks if he's cold enough, and strong enough, and wins enough, Father will love him again. Like before." She shook her head. "I don't want to be like that. I don't want to be cold."
"Then don't be," said Ela.
She said it simply. The way she says everything. The way she'd say *the answer is seven,* or *you're wrong about that.* As if it was the most obvious thing in the world.
"Come with us," said Ela.
Vera looked up, surprised. Her eyes were wet.

I had never seen Ela trust anyone so fast. Ela doesn't trust anyone. Ela didn't trust *me* for the first eight years of my life. But she was standing there in the snow, holding out her hand to Mordecai Vane's daughter.
Vera looked at Ela's hand for a long moment.

"I can't," she said finally. "Not yet. If I run away now, he'll know I've been helping you. He'll know everything. And he'll move your grandmother somewhere I can't find her. Somewhere *nobody* can find her." She took a deep breath. "But I'll keep helping. When I can. I promise."
From the cave, we heard the Grays breaking through the stone. *Crack. Crack.* A piece of the Troll Queen's elbow fell off.
Vera backed away. "Go. Now. I'll tell them you escaped over the glacier. I'll tell them I chased you, and lost you in the snow."
"Vera," I said. "Thank you."
For the first time since I had met her, she smiled. A real smile. Not a snake's smile at all. Not her father's smile, with too many teeth. Just a girl's smile.
"Two to one, Windborn," she said. "Don't lose the next one."
Then she turned and ran back toward the cave.

chapters.t: Chapter Twenty-Eight: Meanwhile, Behind the Trolls
p: *This part Kuzey heard about much, much later. From Vex himself.*
It was dark behind the stone trolls. Completely dark. The sunlight couldn't get past them, and the Grays didn't need light to see, so none of them had flashlights.

Vex sat on the frozen floor of the tunnel with his back against the stone leg of a troll, and listened to the Grays chipping at the rock. *Crack. Crack. Crack.* Slow and steady. They would get through eventually. Grays always got through eventually.
His hands hurt.

They hurt so much. Much more than in Athens, or Crete. He had used the gloves more today than ever before, blasting fog at the trolls, at the Black Wind, at Kuzey. Now, in the dark, he pulled off his right glove and held up his hand in front of his face, even though he couldn't see it.
He didn't need to see it. He could feel it.
His fingertips were stiff and cold. Not cold like skin. Cold like stone. He pressed them against his cheek, and they felt hard. Like pebbles.

The gray marks had spread. He knew they had. He had seen them that morning, in the mirror of the car. Up past the first knuckle of every finger now, on both hands. Gray and hard and cracked, like his father's hand.
Like his father's hand.
He sat there in the dark and thought about that for a long time.
Then he heard footsteps on the other side of the stone. Light footsteps, in the snow. And his sister's voice, through a crack between two trolls.
"Vex? Vex, are you there? Are you okay?"
"I'm fine," he said. His voice came out strange. "Where are they?"
"Gone," said Vera. "Over the glacier. I chased them, but I lost them in the snow. They had a raven. A whole army of ravens. I couldn't keep up."
Vex was quiet for a long time.
"You're lying," he said.
On the other side of the stone, Vera didn't say anything.
"I saw you," said Vex. "In the cave. You shouted at him. About the sun. You told him what to do."
Silence.

Vex pressed his stone fingertips against the stone troll, and closed his eyes. He thought about his father's face, when he heard. He thought about what his father would do to Vera. To his sister. His twin. The only person in the whole world who knew about his hands.
"Vera," he said at last. Very quietly. So the Grays couldn't hear.
"Yes?"
"When Father asks," said Vex, "I'll tell him you chased them over the glacier. And lost them in the snow."
He heard her breath catch.
"Don't," he said. "Just don't. Don't say anything. Just get me out of here."
On the other side of the stone, his sister started to dig.
We drove back west for two days, slowly, carefully, through the snow, stopping whenever Krummi said a road was dangerous, which was often.
On the second day, Krummi said, "KRAA! Stop! Stop the car! Bath time!"
"Bath time?" said Uncle Tarık.
"He says there's a hot river," said Bora. "Up that valley. A secret one. The tourists don't know about it. Only the ravens and the sheep."

We parked by the side of the road and walked up a little valley, through the snow, following the raven. After about half an hour, we heard the sound of water, and saw steam rising between the hills. And there it was.

A river. A small one, about as wide as a road, running down the valley between banks of snow and green moss. And the whole river was steaming. Great clouds of white steam rising off it into the cold air.
Because the water was hot.
Not boiling, like the geysers. Just hot. Like a bath. Warmed by a volcano somewhere deep under the ground, Uncle Tarık said, and pushed up through the rocks.
We looked at each other.
Five minutes later, we were sitting in it.

It was the best feeling of my entire life. After a week of being frozen, of snow and ice and blizzards and glaciers, sitting in a hot river was like being hugged by the whole earth. The water was warm and clear and smelled slightly of eggs. Above us, the sky was blue and cold. Around us, the hills were white. Snowflakes drifted down and melted on our noses.
Bora floated on his back with his arms spread out and his eyes closed. "I'm never leaving," he said. "I live here now. I'm a hot river person. Tell my mother."
Ela sat in the shallows with only her head out of the water, reading a book about Egypt, holding it carefully above the water with both hands. Uncle Tarık had fallen asleep against a rock, snoring.
Krummi sat on the bank, watching us with great disapproval. Ravens don't like baths.
I lay back in the warm water and looked up at the sky, and talked to my winds.

It was different now. With two of them. The Yıldız was the same as always, cold and bright and friendly, like a big white dog. But the Karayel was new. It was wild and moody and strange. It didn't talk much. When it did, it said things like *I don't trust the clouds over there* or *that sheep is looking at us.* It reminded me a bit of Krummi.
But every now and then, I felt it stretch inside me. Like a cat that has been in a box for a long time, stretching out in the sun for the first time.
"Are you happy?" I asked it. "In there? With me?"
The Black Wind thought about it for a long time.
*It is better than the ice,* it said finally. *And you are better than kings.* It paused. *But it is not free. Do not forget.*
"I won't forget," I said. "I promised."
*Yes,* said the Black Wind. *You did.*
The Yıldız stirred, too. *He doesn't forget things,* it said, to the Karayel. *Except his homework.*
I laughed so suddenly that I got hot river water up my nose.
Ela's training program had grown to twenty-three points.

"Point fourteen," she said, standing in the snow outside the little guesthouse where we stayed on the drive back west, with the Clue Book. "Two winds at once. You did it at the glacier, when you blew away the clouds. But you were desperate. You need to be able to do it when you're *not* desperate."
"I'm always a bit desperate," I said.
"That's not a training strategy," said Ela.
So I practiced. In the guesthouse's back garden, in the snow, while Bora and Uncle Tarık watched from the kitchen window, drinking hot chocolate.

It was much harder than one wind. Much, much harder. The Yıldız and the Karayel were so different. When I asked the North Wind to do something, it did it quickly and cleanly, like a well-trained dog. When I asked the Black Wind, it thought about it first. It argued. Sometimes it did something completely different, just to see what would happen.

The first time I tried to use both, I made a tiny blizzard and a tiny thunderstorm at the same time, and they crashed into each other, and the owner's washing line was covered in hailstones the size of marbles.

The second time, the Black Wind made a black cloud, and the North Wind froze it, and it fell out of the sky and hit Ela on the head. It was like being hit with a big black snowball. She was not happy.
"Point fourteen," she said, brushing ice out of her braids, "is still in progress."
The tenth time, though, something happened.
I stopped trying to *make* them work together. I stopped asking them to do the same thing. Instead, I asked them each to do their own thing. The thing they liked best.
"Yıldız," I said. "Could you make something cold and beautiful, please? Something you like?"
"Karayel," I said. "Could you make something wild? Something you like?"
The North Wind made snow. Very fine, very soft snow, falling slowly, every flake perfect, glittering in the light from the kitchen windows.

And the Black Wind took the snow, and spun it. Not violently. Playfully. It spun it into a spiral, a whirling column of glittering snow, rising up from the garden into the dark sky, round and round and round, faster and faster, like a dancer.
A tornado of snow. A small one, as tall as the house, sparkling in the light. Completely silent. Completely beautiful.

In the kitchen window, Bora had his face pressed against the glass. Uncle Tarık had spilled his hot chocolate. The owner of the guesthouse, a big farmer with a red beard, had come out onto the step and was staring with his mouth open.
And Ela, standing in the snow next to me, slowly lowered the Clue Book.
"Okay," she said quietly. "Point fourteen. Complete."
The snow tornado spun for a minute more. Then it slowed down, and fell, and drifted gently down over the garden like glitter, covering everything in a thin layer of new snow.
*That,* said the Black Wind, sounding very pleased with itself, *was fun.*
*Show-off,* said the North Wind.
I laughed. I couldn't help it. They were arguing. Inside me. Like two brothers.
"What's funny?" said Ela.
"Nothing," I said. "They like each other. I think."
On the last morning, we drove back to Þingvellir. The rift. The place where we had met Krummi.
He had told us he wanted to go home.

We stood at the top of the path, where it went down into the crack between the continents. The snow was falling softly. The black rock walls rose up on either side. Krummi sat on Bora's shoulder, his feathers fluffed up against the cold.
Bora had gone quiet. He had been quiet all morning.
"You could come with us," he said, at last. "To Egypt. It's warm there. Lots of food. Lots of... I don't know. Camels. You could talk to the camels."
Krummi made a soft clicking sound in his throat.
"He says camels are very stupid," said Bora, and laughed, but it was a wobbly laugh.
Krummi hopped down off his shoulder onto a rock, so that he could look Bora in the eye.
And then he talked for a long time. A low, soft, croaking sound, very different from his usual screaming. Bora listened, his face very still. Ela and Uncle Tarık and I stood back and waited.
When Krummi finished, Bora wiped his nose on his mitten.

"He says," said Bora, "that Iceland is his home. That the ravens of Þingvellir need him, because he's the cleverest, and without him they'll do something stupid, like try to steal a whole sheep. He says his grandmother lives here, and his cousins, and his old friend the arctic fox who lives under the waterfall." Bora swallowed. "He says I'm the first human who's ever understood him. In his whole life. And he'll never forget me."
Krummi bent his head. With his sharp beak, very carefully, he pulled out one of his own feathers. A long one, from his wing. Black, shining purple and blue in the light.
He held it out to Bora.

"He says," whispered Bora, taking it, "if I ever need help, from any raven, anywhere in the world, show them this. And say Krummi sent me. And they'll help. Because all the ravens in the world know Krummi."
"Of course they do," said Ela softly.
Bora held the feather very carefully, the way you'd hold something made of glass.
"Thank you, Krummi," he said. "You're the best raven in Iceland. In the whole world."
"KRAA," said Krummi. Which Bora didn't need to translate.

The raven spread his huge black wings and took off into the falling snow. He flew down into the rift, between the black walls, low and fast. Then he turned and came back, swooping over our heads, so low that his wings brushed Bora's hat. He circled us three times, croaking.
Then he flew away, up and up, into the gray sky, getting smaller and smaller, until he was just a black dot.
Then he was gone.
Bora stood there looking at the sky for a long time. Then he took off his hat, put the feather carefully inside the lining, and put his hat back on.
He didn't say anything all the way back to Reykjavík. And nobody made him.

chapters.t: Chapter Thirty-Two: Meanwhile, at the Gray Tower
p: *Another part of the story Kuzey heard much later.*
"Two to one," said Mordecai Vane.

He was standing at the window of his map room at the top of the gray tower, with his back to his children. Outside, the fog pressed against the glass, thick and white. The fire in the fireplace gave no heat. It never did, in this tower.
Vex and Vera stood side by side in front of his desk. They hadn't sat down. Their father never asked them to sit down.

"Two to one," said Mordecai again. "The North and the Black. Two winds, inside one boy. And all I have is this." He held up his stone hand. In it, the Lodos Key gleamed dully, cold and gray, like an old spoon. "One frightened wind that won't stop crying."
Nobody said anything.
"Tell me again," said Mordecai, "what happened at the glacier."

"Trolls," said Vex. "Twelve of them. The Grays fought them. The boy got the Key. Then he ran out and the sun came up and the trolls turned to stone. We were trapped in the cave behind them. It took the Grays three hours to dig through."
"And your sister?"
Vex didn't look at Vera. "She was outside. She chased the boy across the glacier. She lost him in the snow. They had ravens."
"Ravens," said Mordecai.
"Hundreds of them," said Vex. "The big kid can talk to animals. He's a Beastspeaker."

For the first time, their father turned around. He looked surprised. "A Beastspeaker? Truly? I haven't heard of one of those in a hundred years." He looked at the cold Key in his stone hand, thoughtfully. "Nermin does choose interesting friends for her grandson."
He walked around the desk. He stood in front of Vera.
He looked down at her for a long time. Vera looked back at him. She didn't blink.
"You lost him in the snow," said her father softly.
"Yes, Father."

"You. Who can find anything. Who found my hidden study when you were seven. Who always knows where I've put my keys." He tilted his head. "You lost three children, a fat professor and an umbrella. In the snow."
"There was a blizzard," said Vera. "And ravens."
Mordecai looked at her for a very long time.

Then he reached out with his human hand, his left hand, the one that was still skin and bone, and he took her wrist. Gently. Very gently. He turned it over. He looked at the thin silver bracelet she always wore, with the little gray stone in it.
He touched the gray stone with one finger.
"You still wear your mother's bracelet," he said.
"Always," said Vera.
"Good," said her father quietly. "Good. Keep it on. Wherever you go." He let go of her wrist. "It keeps you safe."
He turned back to the window.
"Go to bed. Both of you. We'll talk tomorrow about Egypt."
On the stairs, Vera stopped. She held up her wrist and looked at the bracelet in the dim light. At the little gray stone.
*It keeps you safe.*
She stood there for a long time. Then she pulled her sleeve down over it, and kept walking.

Below her on the stairs, her brother was waiting. He didn't say anything. He just looked at her. Then he looked at the sleeve over her wrist. Then he turned and walked down the stairs ahead of her, without a word.
But Vera had seen his face.
He was thinking the same thing she was.
Guðrún was waiting for us in the doorway of her little red house, with her arms folded and her braids under a woolly hat.
"You're late," she said. "The soup has been ready for an hour."

She fed us so much that night that even Bora had to lie down afterward. Lamb soup, smoked fish, rye bread baked in the hot ground by a geyser, pancakes with cream and jam, and more skyr with blueberries. She didn't offer us any more fermented shark. Bora said he was "a bit disappointed, actually," and Ela threw a cushion at him.
After dinner, Guðrún sat in her chair by the fire, and looked at me with her bright blue eyes.
"You found it," she said. It wasn't a question.
I breathed out. A tiny black cloud floated across the room and rained a little bit on her carpet.
Guðrún looked at it for a long time. Then she smiled, and her whole face crinkled up.

"Your grandmother," she said, "sat in that chair, forty-five years ago, and did exactly the same thing. Except it was snow. It made a little snowman on the rug." She laughed. "Very small. I kept it in the freezer for two years."
"Grandma isn't a Windborn," I said. "She said so."

"No," said Guðrún. "But she was carrying the North Wind for the Order. In the Yıldız Key. On her necklace. Taking it to Istanbul, to keep it safe. And sometimes, when you carry a wind for long enough, it starts to like you." She leaned forward. "The winds have loved your family for a very long time, Kuzey Aydın. Don't forget that."
That night, in Guðrún's little guest room, we spread out the leather map on the bed.
Three stars were dark now. Istanbul. Crete. Iceland.
And a new one was glowing. Warm and gold. Far to the south. In the desert, by a long green river.

"Egypt," said Uncle Tarık. And a slow smile spread across his face. "I've always wanted to dig in Egypt. Ever since I was a little boy. I had a poster of the Sphinx on my wall." He looked a bit embarrassed. "I still have it."
Ela was writing in the Clue Book. A new page.
*SCORE*
*Kuzey: 2 (Yıldız, Karayel)*
*Mordecai: 1 (Lodos)*
*Keys left: 4*
*New friends: Guðrún, Krummi, Sóley the horse, the hot river (does a river count?)*
*Vera: definitely helping. Probably. 85%.*
"Eighty-five percent?" I said.
"She saved us from twelve trolls," said Ela. "I've gone up from sixty."
Bora was sitting by the window with his hat on, even though we were inside. Krummi's feather was in it.
"Kuzey," he said. "Look."

I went to the window. Outside, over the dark roofs of Reykjavík, the northern lights were dancing. Green and purple and pink, rippling across the sky, the way they had on our first night. The way they had when Mordecai's face had appeared in them.
I held my breath.
But this time, they didn't make a face with too many teeth.
They swirled together, slowly, in the middle of the sky. Green and gold and silver. And they made a shape. Seven points. Like a star. Like a compass rose. One point longer than the others.
Pointing south.

*Go well, Windborn,* rumbled the big wind of Iceland, very softly, from somewhere high above the lights. *Go south. To the sand and the sun. Your Black Wind and your North Wind will keep you cold enough.*
"Thank you," I whispered. "For everything."
*Come back one day,* said the wind. *When it is over. When we are all free. Come back and visit. Bring the big one. The ravens liked him.*
Bora was smiling.
The lights shimmered and faded, slowly, and the stars came out, millions of them, over the little red houses of Reykjavík.
§END To be continued in Book Four: The Sphinx's Second Riddle.

For hundreds of years, sailors on the Black Sea, the Bosphorus and the Mediterranean used a wind rose to name the winds. Each wind had its own name and its own personality, and every sailor knew them by heart. These are the seven winds of the Order of the Compass Rose.
**Yıldız (North).** Named after the North Star, *yıldız* means "star." A cold, clear, starry wind. Kuzey's own wind.
**Poyraz (Northeast).** The great wind of the Black Sea. When the Poyraz blows hard, the fishermen go home and the ferries rock.
**Gündoğusu (East).** "Sunrise." The wind that comes from where the sun is born each morning.
**Keşişleme (Southeast).** Named after the monks, the *keşiş,* who lived on the mountains to the southeast. A warm, dry wind from the deserts.
**Kıble (South).** The wind from the direction of Mecca. Hot, and full of sand.
**Lodos (Southwest).** A warm, wild, wet wind that brings big waves and headaches. People in Istanbul say the Lodos makes everyone grumpy.
**Karayel (Northwest).** "Black wind." A stormy, dark wind that brings clouds and sudden rain.
And the eighth, the west wind, the **Batı**, the one that would not make a deal? Nobody knows. It is still wild. That is another story.

chapters.t: The Real Places in This Book
p: **Reykjavík's swimming pools.** Icelanders really do go swimming outdoors all year round, in pools heated by volcanoes, with hot pots for sitting and talking.
**Hákarl.** Fermented shark is a real traditional Icelandic food. It really does smell terrible.

**Þingvellir.** A real rift valley, where the North American and Eurasian plates are pulling apart by about two centimeters a year. The Vikings held their parliament, the Althing, there from the year 930. It's one of the oldest parliaments in the world.
**Ravens.** Iceland's ravens are big, clever and famous in Icelandic folklore. Icelanders really do call them *krummi.*
**Strokkur.** A real geyser, in a valley full of steam and bubbling pools. It erupts every few minutes, shooting boiling water up to 20 meters or more into the air.
**Icelandic horses.** Small, tough, shaggy and very friendly. They've lived in Iceland since the Vikings brought them over a thousand years ago.

**Reynisfjara.** The black sand beach near Vík, with basalt columns and three sea stacks that legend says were trolls caught by the sunrise. Sneaker waves there are real and very dangerous. Never turn your back on the sea.
**Jökulsárlón.** A real lagoon full of icebergs at the foot of a glacier. Seals really do swim between the icebergs.
**Vatnajökull.** The biggest ice cap in Iceland, with volcanoes underneath it, and blue ice caves you can visit in winter, with a guide.
**Trolls and the Yule Lads.** From Icelandic folklore. In the old stories, trolls really do turn to stone in the sun.
*Here is the first chapter of the next book,* The Sphinx's Second Riddle.
**Chapter One: Sand in Everything**
From Iceland to Egypt is a jump from minus ten degrees to plus thirty. My body didn't know what was happening.

I stepped out of Cairo airport into a wall of heat. Hot, dry, dusty heat, like opening an oven. The North Wind and the Black Wind both panicked inside me. The North Wind wanted to freeze everything. The Black Wind wanted to make a storm. They argued about it so loudly in my head that I didn't notice the sneeze coming.
"A-a-a-CHOO!"
I sneezed a tiny snowstorm onto a taxi driver.
It wasn't a big one. Just a little cloud of snowflakes, glittering in the sunshine, swirling around his head and settling on his mustache and his eyebrows and the top of his taxi.
"Sorry!" I said. "Allergies!"

He looked at the snowflakes melting on his mustache. He looked at the blue Egyptian sky, with not a single cloud in it. He looked at me. Then he said something in Arabic that sounded like a prayer, put our bags in his taxi very quickly, and drove us very fast to our hotel without saying another word.
"Allergies?" said Ela, in the back seat. "*Allergies?*"
"It's what Bora's mom says whenever he sneezes on someone."
"Bora's mom," said Bora, "is a very wise woman."

Cairo is the biggest city I have ever seen. Bigger than Istanbul, which I didn't think was possible. Twenty million people. A million car horns, all honking at the same time, all day and all night. Donkey carts next to brand-new cars. Men on bicycles carrying huge trays of bread on their heads, steering through the traffic with one hand. Buildings in every color of sand, from pale yellow to dark brown, stretching away to the horizon, with thousands of minarets rising above them.
And the Nile flowing through the middle of it all, wide and brown and slow, with little white sailboats drifting on it.
And at the edge of the city, rising out of the desert like mountains someone built on purpose, the pyramids.

I saw them from the taxi window, as we came over a bridge. Three of them. Huge and golden and perfect, standing at the edge of the city where the houses stopped and the desert began, shimmering in the heat.
Uncle Tarık saw them too. He made a sound like a whimper.

"The Great Pyramid," he said. He had tears in his eyes. Actual tears. "Four thousand five hundred years old. For almost four thousand years, it was the tallest building on Earth. Kids, this is the best day of my life."
"You said that in Athens," said Ela.
"And Iceland," said Bora.
"I have many best days," said Uncle Tarık happily, wiping his eyes.

The desert wind came in through the taxi window, and it was different from every wind I had met so far. Hot and dry, with a voice like rustling paper. Like pages turning in an old book. It didn't argue, like the Greek winds, or rumble, like the Icelandic ones. It *whispered secrets.* Thousands of them, all at the same time, overlapping, hissing, like sand pouring through fingers.

*The sand remembers,* it hissed. *The sand remembers everything. The pharaohs. The builders. The slaves. The kings. The thieves. The silver-haired woman who came forty years ago and hid a wind in the place of riddles.*
"The place of riddles," I repeated. "Grandma was here. Forty years ago. She hid the Keşişleme somewhere with riddles."
"The Keşişleme," said Ela, writing. "The southeast wind. The wind from the deserts."
She looked out of the window, toward the pyramids. In front of them, small from this distance, crouched a shape. A lion, lying down, with its paws stretched out in front of it. And a human head.
"Only one place in Egypt," she said, "is famous for riddles."
§END To be continued in* The Sphinx's Second Riddle...
